notes:
I've gathered notes for most verses, but the research has gaps you should know about first:

- **Missing sources:** I ran out of search and fetch attempts. I couldn't open the NET Bible notes, any Catholic or Orthodox page, or any page on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching about this chapter.
- **Verses 20–23:** The Enduring Word page cut off at verse 20, so these verses have little or nothing.
- **Tradition labels:** The labels in brackets (Calvin as Reformed, Gill as Baptist, Clarke as Methodist, Ellicott as Anglican) are my own. The pages I read don't state them, so check them before printing.

**v. 1**
- This Herod is Herod Agrippa I. Guzik calls him the grandson of Herod the Great and the nephew of Herod Antipas, and says he harassed the church because it was politically popular. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- The events date to about AD 43–44, since that is when Herod died. Luke is deliberately vague about timing, and scholars disagree on the order of events in Acts 10–12 (Stott). https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary
- Matthew Henry reads "stretched forth his hands" as Herod pushing past the restraints that had held him back. He started with harassment and moved on to worse cruelty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary
- A.T. Robertson says this is the first time since Pilate that political power is used against the disciples. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary
- **Modern scholarship (NET note, as quoted by Precept Austin):** this persecution ended a short period of peace noted in Acts 9:31. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary

**v. 2**
- James was the first of the Twelve to be martyred. His death showed that the apostles had no special protection. It fulfilled Jesus' words about drinking His cup (Mark 10:35–40). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- "With the sword" usually means beheading. Eusebius passes on a story from Clement of Alexandria: the guard who brought James to trial confessed Christ and was executed with him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- No one replaced James, unlike Judas, because James died faithful. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/

**v. 3**
- Herod acted from political motives, unlike Saul, who persecuted from misguided religious conviction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- This was Peter's third arrest (Acts 4:3; 5:18). The festival gave Agrippa a chance to win favour with the Jewish crowds (Robertson). https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary
- The Biblical Illustrator: religion was the excuse, but the real cause was Herod's hold on his crown. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-12.html
- John Phillips sees this as a comment on the Jews' rejection of Christ as much as on Herod. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62060/

**v. 4**
- Why wait until after Passover? Horton gives three possible reasons: to look devout, to avoid a riot while pilgrims were in town, or to have everyone's full attention. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- Precept Austin adds that Jewish law did not allow executions during Passover. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary
- Matthew Henry gives two options: Herod feared the crowd might demand Peter's release under the festival custom, or he wanted a public show once the feast was over. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_012.cfm
- The guard was four soldiers per squad, sixteen in all, likely because of Peter's earlier escape (5:19) (Robertson). Most commentators place the prison in the Fortress Antonia. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary

**v. 5**
- Herod had soldiers and prisons, but the church had prayer. "When every other gate is shut and locked, the gate to heaven is wide open" (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- The word for "fervently" or "constant" pictures stretching to the limit (MacArthur). Luke uses the same word for Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane. Guzik adds that earnest prayer doesn't talk a reluctant God round; it shows we care about what God cares about. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- The Biblical Illustrator pictures prayer in relays, the church setting "pickets" as Herod set sentries. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/acts-12.html

**v. 6**
- Peter slept calmly the night before his planned execution (Psalm 127:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- McGarvey: Peter was chained to a soldier on each side, so he could not move without waking one of them. https://www.ccel.org/m/mcgarvey/oca/OCA12.HTM
- Matthew Henry: rescue came on the very last night, which made the comfort to his friends and the confusion of his enemies all the greater. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_012.cfm

**vv. 7–10**
- Chains, guards and gates meant nothing to God. The gate opened "of its own accord" (Greek *automatē*, "automatically"). Guzik's application: don't worry about the iron gate before you reach it. He also retells Bruce's story of Sundar Singh being freed from a well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- Peter did nothing to rescue himself; he was asleep. All he could say was that the Lord led him out (12:17). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62060/

**v. 9**
- Robertson contrasts this with Peter's vision at Joppa. Here Luke presents the event as objective fact. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-12.html

**v. 11**
- Why James died and Peter was spared is often known only to God. It simply wasn't Peter's time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/

**v. 12**
- Robertson suggests Luke may have learned this story from John Mark, since the believers met at his mother's house. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-12.html

**vv. 13–14**
- Rhoda leaving Peter at the gate is a true-to-life detail that Guzik takes as a sign Acts is reliable history. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- The BibleHub study notes compare her to the women who first witnessed the resurrection: God often uses unexpected people. https://biblehub.com/study/acts/12-15.htm

**v. 15** (the clearest disagreement in the chapter)
- **The believers' reaction:** they prayed earnestly but believed weakly, and "little faith can accomplish great things if it is placed in the great God" (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- Barnes says they reached for any explanation except the obvious one. The news seemed too good to be true. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html

What "his angel" means:
- **Calvin [Reformed]:** he accepts that the angel is the one God appointed to keep Peter. But he calls the common conclusion that every person has a particular angel "too weak." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html
- **Gill [Baptist]:** not a personal guardian angel, since sometimes one angel serves many people and many angels guard one saint. Rather, an angel in Peter's shape with a message. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html
- **Matthew Henry:** we know saints have a guard of angels, so there's no need to insist each has his own. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html
- **Clarke [Methodist]:** this was a common Jewish belief, and he notes that in the "popish Church" it is an article of faith. This is a Protestant description of Catholic teaching, not a Catholic source. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html
- **Coffman:** the verse shows the apostolic church believed everyone has a guardian angel, backed by Matthew 18:10. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html
- **Ellicott [Anglican]:** an offhand remark like this cannot count as official approval of the belief. https://biblehub.com/acts/12-15.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** probably a guardian angel, but the phrase is obscure. https://biblehub.com/acts/12-15.htm
- **Constable:** lists three options: a guardian angel, a human messenger sent by Peter, or Peter's spirit after death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-15.html
- **Guzik:** Matthew 18:10 says "angels," plural, and calls them God's angels, not ours. We are never told to give angels orders. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/do-we-have-guardian-angels-qa-for-august-19-2021/

**v. 17**
- The James here is probably the Lord's brother, not the apostle just killed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-12/
- "Another place": Robertson thinks Luke probably didn't know where, and Peter wisely kept it hidden. He is back in Acts 15. Robertson says we do not know whether Peter went to Rome during these years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-12.html
- Arnold: going into hiding was wisdom, not cowardice. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary

**vv. 18–19**
- "No small commotion" is an understatement figure of speech (Constable). Under Roman practice, guards who let a prisoner escape received his penalty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/12-19.html
- Robertson: this was routine Roman practice, not special cruelty by Herod. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-12.html
- McGarvey disagrees: Herod must have known the escape was a miracle, so the executions were "insane fury." https://www.ccel.org/m/mcgarvey/oca/OCA12.HTM
- Henry mentions some who think the guards were sentenced but never executed, because Herod died first. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_012.cfm

**v. 23**
- One angel of the Lord frees a God-fearing man; another strikes down a man who pretends to be a god. The verdict and the sentence came at the same moment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary

**v. 24**
- The chapter opens with James dead, Peter in prison and Herod triumphant. It ends with Herod dead, Peter free and the word of God triumphant. Steven Cole: the gospel can't be stopped. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-12-commentary

**v. 25**
- The chapter's events are set between the arrival of Barnabas and Saul in Jerusalem and their return to Antioch. They were probably in Jerusalem at the feast while Peter was in prison (McGarvey). https://www.ccel.org/m/mcgarvey/oca/OCA12.HTM
